hints: Focus on the two reactants together, the ammonium ion $\text{NH}_4^+$ and hydroxide ion $\text{OH}^-$, and ask what one gives to the other.
Write the key ionic change as $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ and notice it is proton transfer.
Check for the other types by asking if any solid forms, if any oxidation number changes, and if heat alone is causing the breakdown.
walkthrough:
**Spot the acid and the base**

Think of $\text{NH}_4^+$ as an acid because it can donate a proton ($\text{H}^+$). Think of $\text{OH}^-$ from sodium hydroxide as a classic base that accepts a proton.

Key idea:
$$\text{acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor}$$

**Write what actually happens**

When warmed, the two react together to release ammonia gas. Heating just speeds it up and drives off the $\text{NH}_3$.

Full equation:
$$(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Rule out the other reaction types**

No insoluble solid is made, so it is not precipitation. Oxidation numbers stay the same ($\text{N}$ is -3 in both $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{NH}_3$), so it is not redox. It needs the $\text{NaOH}$ reactant, so it is not thermal decomposition by heat alone. That leaves proton transfer, which is acid-base.

options.A: Correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ donates $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{OH}^-$, giving $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. This proton transfer is the definition of a Bronsted-Lowry acid-base reaction.
options.B: Not correct. Precipitation needs an insoluble solid product. Here $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$ is soluble, $\text{NH}_3$ is a gas and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is liquid, so no precipitate forms.
options.C: Not correct. Redox needs a change in oxidation number. Nitrogen stays at -3, sulfur stays at +6, sodium stays at +1, so no electron transfer occurs.
options.D: Not correct. Thermal decomposition is breakdown by heat alone, like a carbonate to oxide plus carbon dioxide. Here reaction only happens because $\text{NaOH}$ is added as a second reactant, with heat just helping release ammonia.
